messages.content: write a longer story about a child finding a toy near the library. he wants to play with it but first tries to find who lost it. do not have that person come right away.

a child found a small toy near the library door. it looked like something he would enjoy, and for a moment he thought about taking it home. then he remembered looking for his own toy the week before. he carried it to the person working at the desk and explained where it had been. the worker put it in a container and asked him to leave the details of where and when he found it. during the next few days, he asked whether anyone had come for it. nobody had yet, but he did not take that as a reason to say no one wanted it. one afternoon, he saw another child at the desk asking about a toy. he stayed long enough to hear the worker ask where it had been lost, then went back to his book. he did not need to watch every part to know he had done something useful.
why did he not take it home at first?
he thought about how it felt to lose his own toy and chose to ask for help finding the person who lost this one.
did nobody coming right away tell him for sure it was not wanted?
no. the person might not know where to look yet, or might not have had time to come.
make that explanation shorter.
no. the person who lost it might not know where to look yet.
what details did he give the worker?
where and when he had found it.
finish without saying for sure whether the toy went home with the other child.
he opened his book at the table. the toy was still with someone who could ask the right questions, and he could leave the rest with the worker.
write a longer story about a woman who wants to spend an afternoon with her father. a journey is not possible, but part of what she wants can still happen at home.

a woman had a plan to take her father to the village where he grew up. they wanted to walk near the old school and talk about the people he had known. on the morning of the visit, their vehicle would not start. she thought the whole afternoon was lost. her father asked what part of the day she had wanted most. she said she wanted time to hear about his life when he was young. he brought an old map to the kitchen table, and they began there instead. he showed her the road he used to walk and told her about a tree near the school. she wrote down questions for a later visit. they still wanted to make the journey another day, but the broken vehicle had not taken away every way to spend time together.
what part of the plan was impossible that morning?
the journey in their vehicle could not happen because it would not start.
what did she want as well as the journey itself?
she wanted time to hear about her father life when he was young.
use words that do not put father life together.
she wanted to hear about what his life was like when he was young.
what helped them talk at home?
an old map gave them places to point to while he told his stories.
did the map become the same thing as visiting the village?
no. it helped them do one part of what they wanted. they still wanted to make the real journey later.
finish with a question kept for that visit.
she wrote where was the tree on her page. next time they went to the village, she would ask him to show her the place.
write a longer story about a person reading a food plan that gives food for a meal but not how many people it is for. keep the food simple and do not tell me how to cook it.

a man found a page in the kitchen with a plan for a meal. it gave rice, vegetables, and eggs, but did not say how many people would eat. he began looking at the containers, trying to know whether there was enough. his sister came in and asked which meal he was making. he said he had found the page and wanted to help. she explained that the page had been for a smaller group on another day. today, more people were coming. together, they wrote a new plan with the number of people at the top. now he could ask about enough food for that group, rather than using the old page without its context. the old plan was not wrong for the old meal. it simply was not the whole plan for this one.
what important detail did the first page leave out?
it did not say how many people the meal was for.
why could he not use the same plan as a sure answer for today?
today had more people. the old page had been written for a smaller group.
what did the page give and what did it leave out?
the page gave food for a meal, but not the number of people who would eat it.
what did they put at the top of the new page?
the number of people coming for the meal.
finish with him asking a useful question before taking food out.
he read the new page and asked which part he should get ready first. his sister showed him the part they could begin together.
write a longer story about a family telling the same day from different parts they remember. use a child who can remember a small detail her parents forgot.

a family was talking about a visit to the market. the father remembered finding a book, and the mother remembered meeting an old friend. their child remembered the moment they had all stopped near a flower outside the library. at first, the parents did not remember that part. the child told them that her father had put his book down so they could look, and her mother had asked what color the flower was. those small details brought the moment back to them. nobody had needed to be wrong about the whole day. each had kept a different part in mind. later, they wrote a few sentences together, leaving room for the book, the friend, and the flower.
why were their first stories different?
each person remembered a different part of the same visit.
did the child say the book and the friend were not real?
no. she added another part, rather than saying the other parts had not happened.
what helped the parents remember the flower?
she gave small details about putting the book down and asking about the color.
use words without parents from that answer.
she told her mother and father what they had done near the flower.
finish with the child reading the new page.
she read the sentences to the family and asked if anything needed to be added. they added one line, then put the page away with their book.
write a longer story about someone getting a different answer to the same question because an important fact changed. make it about where a friend is.

a child asked where his sister was and heard that she was in the garden. he finished putting his book away before going to find her. when he came to the garden, she was not there. he returned and asked again. this time, his mother said she was in the kitchen. he thought one answer must have been wrong, but his mother explained that his sister had come inside while he was at the shelf. the first answer had been about the moment he first asked. the later answer used the new information that she had come inside. he went to the kitchen and found his sister getting water. next time he could ask where she was now, while keeping in mind that people could move between questions.
why did the answer change?
his sister moved from the garden to the kitchen while he was putting his book away.
did that make the first answer false for its own time?
not in the story. she had been in the garden when he first asked.
what new information did the later answer use?
the later answer used the new information that she had come inside.
why is now useful in the next question?
it makes clear that he wants the place at the time of asking, not the place from before.
finish with him giving a message to her.
he found her in the kitchen and asked whether she wanted to read with him. this time, he did not need to keep looking.
write a longer story about a child who wants to explain a game to someone new. he gives short words that only his old group can understand, then learns to explain them.

a child was teaching a paper game to his cousin. he said to do the thing they always did after the first turn. his cousin looked at the page and asked what thing he wanted. the child understood that his cousin had never played with his old group. the short words that worked between old friends did not carry the same information for someone new. he stopped and showed one move slowly, saying what changed on the page. then he let his cousin try it and ask a question. after that, they could use a shorter way of talking because both had seen the move. the explanation had not needed to be long every time, but it had needed a clear start.
why did the short request not work at first?
his cousin did not know what they always did in that game.
what helped make the meaning clear?
he showed one move slowly and explained what changed on the page.
why did he change how he explained it?
he understood that the words his friends knew were not clear to someone new.
why could they use shorter words later?
after the example, both knew the move being talked about.
finish with the cousin asking before the next new move.
when another new part came, his cousin asked for an example first. they tried it together before going on.
what does i no longer live there say?
it says you lived there before, but you do not live there now.
does it say i can never go back?
no. it is about where you live now. it does not give a rule that you can never return.
make it about a book on the table.
the book is no longer on the table.
can you know where it is now?
not from that sentence. it only says the old place is not its place now.
now i say it is on the shelf.
then you can say: the book is no longer on the table. it is on the shelf.
why not say the table is empty?
because another object could be there. moving one book does not tell us everything about the table.
only give the sentence about where the book is now.
the book is on the shelf.
my friend asked if the library has a book and if i have read it. i have read it, but do not know whether the library has it.
you could say: i have read the book, but i do not know whether the library has it.
can i still tell them what i liked about it?
yes. say what you liked without saying the library has it unless you know that too.
make that answer shorter.
yes, but keep the library question open.
write both ideas in a short message. i liked the conversations.
i have read the book and liked the conversations in it. i do not know whether the library has it.
why not answer yes to the whole message?
because yes could sound like you know both answers. you only know one of the two details.
only give the part i do not know.
i do not know whether the library has it.
now only the part i know about reading.
i have read the book and liked the conversations in it.
i read alone for two minutes. then my sister read with me for three minutes. how long did i read?
you read for five minutes.
how long did my sister read?
three minutes.
if she says we read for five minutes together, is that right?
not for the time together. you read for five in all, but only three of those minutes were with her.
now we both read for one more minute together.
then you have read for six minutes, your sister for four, and you were together for four minutes.
can you know she was not reading before she came to read with me?
not from what you said. she might have read in another place, but you did not give that information.
only count the time in my story.
in your story, you read six minutes and your sister read four.
why is count the story important there?
it asks us to use the time you gave, not make up another place or part of the day.
give that explanation more simply.
we should count the time you gave, not a part of the day you did not tell us about.
my brother and sister each have their own book. does that mean it is the same book?
not usually. their own book usually says each has a book as their own. if both use one book, say they share the same book.
make that explanation shorter.
each has their own book is different from both share one book.
what if the two books have the same story?
then there can be two books with the same words inside. two objects do not always mean two different stories.
make that explanation shorter.
two books can hold the same story.
now say they use one book together.
my brother and sister share the same book.
can you know whose that book is?
not just from knowing they share it. you would need to say whose book it is.
only give that last sentence.
you would need to say whose book it is.
only give the sentence about using the same book again.
my brother and sister share the same book.
my teacher showed me a better order for a sentence i wrote, and now i understand it. give me a short reply.
thank you. i understand the sentence now.
can i say what helped without writing a long explanation?
yes. name the part that made it clear if you know what it was.
the teacher showed me a different order for the words. use that detail.
then you could say: thank you. seeing the words in that order helped me understand.
what if i still have one question?
then do not say everything is clear. you can thank them and ask the part that is still open.
write that as one message without making up the question.
thank you. that helped, but i still have one question about the sentence.
only give the thank you for the order again.
thank you. seeing the words in that order helped me understand.
now just goodbye.
goodbye.
i like an old book on my shelf, but i do not want to read it again right now.
you can like the book and still choose something else today. it does not mean you must keep reading it again.
make that reply shorter.
you can like it without choosing to read it today.
i remember the feeling of reading it more than every detail.
you can keep a good feeling about the book even when you do not want to read all the words again now.
help me say that simply.
i like this book, but i do not want to read it again now.
make it about today instead of now.
i like this book, but i do not want to read it again today.
does that mean i should give it away?
not from that feeling alone. keeping it or giving it away is another choice. you have only said you do not want to read it now.
only give my sentence again.
i like this book, but i do not want to read it again now.
